# Mahāsaḷāyatanika Sutta (MN 149 (PTS MN iii 287))

**ID:** MN 149 (PTS MN iii 287)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Mahāsaḷāyatanika Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** The Great Discourse on What Relates to the Six Sense Fields
**PTS:** MN iii 287
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāsaḷāyatanika Sutta* (MN 149), delivered by the Buddha at Jeta's Grove in Anāthapiṇḍika's Park at Sāvatthi, outlines how insight into the six sense-doors is integrated with the noble eightfold path and culminates in liberation [Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. The discourse contrasts two experiential modes: failing to know and see as they truly are (*ajānam apassam yathābhūtaṁ*) the internal and external sense bases, consciousness, contact (*samphassa*), and the resultant feelings leads to infatuation (*sārajjati*), the growth of defilements, and future bondage [Gethin 2001; Wen 2009; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. In contrast, seeing them according to reality abandons lust and directly unfolds the path of awakening [Wen 2009; Anālayo 2006].

When a practitioner stays aloof from infatuation regarding sense experience and affective feelings, five path factors—right view, right intention, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—naturally arise and develop, supported by the prior purification of right speech, right action, and right livelihood [Gethin 2001; Anālayo 2006]. The sutta explains that this contemplative process simultaneously matures all thirty-seven aids to awakening (*bodhipakkhiyā dhammā*), including the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and the seven enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*) [Gethin 2001; Anālayo 2006; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. It further demonstrates that through this practice, tranquillity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) are cultivated together in balance and operate concurrently [Saitanaporn 2009; Melnikova 2014; Anālayo 2014].

 The discourse is additionally cited in the *Kathāvatthu* (Kv 20.5, *Maggakathā*). DharmaNexus records 1,439 Pali-internal reuse passages across 94 texts, exhibiting massive overlaps with the *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35) and the *Magga Saṁyutta* (SN 45), as well as doctrinal parallels with the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī* (*Dukanikkhepa*), the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* (*Ñāṇakathā*), and the *Vinaya* (*Mahākhandhaka*) [DharmaNexus]. Cross-language alignments computed by DharmaNexus include citations in the Tibetan *Abhidharmakośaṭīkopayikā* (D4094) and *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (D4049), as well as the Sanskrit *Arthaviniścayasūtra* commentary [DharmaNexus].
